bill.title: Veterans 2nd Amendment Protection Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Hearings held. Hearings printed: S.Hrg. 119-35.
bill.officialSummary: Veterans 2nd Amendment Protection Act of 2025 This bill prohibits the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) from transmitting certain information to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) utilized by licensed importers or dealers of firearms. Specifically, the bill prohibits the VA from transmitting personally identifying information of a veteran or a beneficiary to the NICS solely on the basis that such veteran or beneficiary has an appointed fiduciary to manage their benefits, unless there is an order or finding of a judicial authority that such veteran or beneficiary is a danger to themselves or others.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would prevent the Department of Veterans Affairs from sending information about veterans or their beneficiaries to the national firearm background-check database solely because they have someone appointed to manage their benefits. The VA could still share such information if a court has found the person to be a danger to themselves or others.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects the National Instant Criminal Background Check System used by licensed firearm dealers and importers.
Organizations focused on Second Amendment rights and veterans' advocacy have a direct stake in policies governing firearm access for veterans.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would ban the VA from transmitting certain information to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System used by licensed importers or dealers of firearms.
plain.whoItTouches: People who own or buy guns. Veterans and their families.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in buying and owning a gun. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
